objectives: Connect to maximum likelihood + Bayesian inference.

slides.title: Mutual information: shared structure between X + Y
slides.body:
**Mutual information** I(X; Y): how much knowing Y reduces uncertainty about X (or vice versa).

  I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y)

• I(X; Y) ≥ 0; equals 0 iff X ⊥ Y.
• Symmetric: I(X; Y) = I(Y; X).
• Bounded: I(X; Y) ≤ min(H(X), H(Y)).

**Interpretations**:
- Bits of information about X obtainable from Y on average.
- Bits saved when encoding X knowing Y vs not knowing.
- Tightness of dependence (deterministic Y = f(X) → I = H(X)).
- Generalized correlation (works for non-linear, categorical, mixed-type).

**Examples**:
- Coin flip + its outcome: I = 1 bit (knowing outcome fully informs).
- Coin flip + an unrelated coin flip: I = 0.
- Coin flip + 'flipper's mood': probably low I.
- Stock price + news sentiment: small but non-zero I (correlated weakly).
- Coordinates of nearby trees in a forest: high I (spatial structure).

**Data processing inequality**: information cannot be created by processing.
  X → Y → Z (Markov chain) ⟹ I(X; Z) ≤ I(X; Y).

**Applications**:
- **Feature selection**: pick features with high I to predict label.
- **Independent component analysis (ICA)**: minimize MI between components.
- **Variational inference**: ELBO = -KL(q || p_post) = expected log-likelihood + mutual information term.
- **Channel capacity**: C = max I(X; Y) over input distribution (next lesson).
- **Representation learning**: maximize I between input + representation while constraining (info bottleneck).

slides.title: KL divergence: measuring difference between distributions
slides.body:
**Kullback-Leibler divergence** (1951):

  D_KL(P || Q) = ∑ P(x) log[P(x)/Q(x)]   (discrete)
  D_KL(P || Q) = ∫ P(x) log[P(x)/Q(x)] dx  (continuous)

Properties:
• D_KL(P || Q) ≥ 0; equals 0 iff P = Q.
• **Not symmetric**: D_KL(P || Q) ≠ D_KL(Q || P) in general.
• **Not a metric**: doesn't satisfy triangle inequality.
• Diverges when Q(x) = 0 + P(x) > 0 for any x.
• Units: bits (log₂) or nats (ln).

**Interpretations**:
- 'Information lost' when approximating P with Q.
- Inefficiency of coding P-distributed data with code optimized for Q.
- Likelihood ratio: D_KL(P || Q) = E_P[log(P/Q)] = relative entropy.
- Forward KL vs Reverse KL:
  - Forward D_KL(P || Q): penalty for Q underestimating P (Q must cover P's support). 'Inclusive.'
  - Reverse D_KL(Q || P): penalty for Q exceeding P (Q can ignore parts). 'Exclusive,' mode-seeking.
  - VAE training: minimizes D_KL(q || p) — encoder q seeks mode of true posterior p.

**Connection to mutual information**: I(X; Y) = D_KL(p(x,y) || p(x) p(y)) — divergence between joint + product of marginals. Zero iff X ⊥ Y.

**Cross-entropy**: H(P, Q) = -∑ P log Q = H(P) + D_KL(P || Q). Used in ML as the **cross-entropy loss** (negative log-likelihood).

**Jensen-Shannon divergence**: symmetric variant: JS(P, Q) = ½ [D_KL(P || M) + D_KL(Q || M)], where M = (P+Q)/2. Bounded, symmetric, useful when KL diverges.

**f-divergences**: family generalizing KL (Csiszár 1967). KL, JS, Hellinger, χ², total variation all special cases. Each has different sensitivity profile. Used in: GANs (Jensen-Shannon, then Wasserstein); domain adaptation; statistical testing.

slides.title: Information bottleneck + ML connections
slides.body:
**Information bottleneck** (Tishby 1999): for a learning task, find representation T that maximizes I(T; Y) (predictive) while minimizing I(T; X) (compressed). Lagrangian:

  L = I(T; Y) - β I(T; X)

β controls tradeoff. Lower β: more compression but loss of predictive power.

**Interpretation in deep learning**:
- Each hidden layer is a representation T.
- During training, layers move toward higher I(T; Y) (fitting).
- Then 'compression phase': I(T; X) decreases as layer becomes invariant to irrelevant input variations.
- Initially controversial but emerging as theoretical lens for deep-learning generalization (Schwartz-Ziv & Tishby 2017; Saxe+ 2018; many follow-ups).

**Cross-entropy loss + KL divergence**: standard classification loss is cross-entropy:
  L = -∑ y_i log p_θ(x)_i = H(P_true, P_θ)

Minimizing cross-entropy = minimizing KL(P_true || P_θ) + H(P_true) — the H is constant in θ; the KL is what's minimized.

**Variational inference**: ELBO = log p(x) - D_KL(q(z|x) || p(z|x)) where:
- p(z|x): true (intractable) posterior.
- q(z|x): variational approximation.
- Minimize KL → maximize ELBO.
- VAE training uses this with KL(q || prior) penalty for regularization.

**Mutual information neural estimation (MINE)**: Belghazi+ 2018 + variants estimate MI via deep networks. Used for: representation-learning objectives, fairness constraints, contrastive learning.

**InfoNCE objective** (CPC, SimCLR, CLIP): maximize MI between input + representation using contrastive samples. Foundation of modern self-supervised learning.

**Conditional MI + transfer**: I(X; Y | Z) measures dependence beyond what Z explains. Useful for: causal inference (confounding by Z), explainable AI (feature attribution), partial information decomposition.

**Information geometry** (Amari 1985, Amari + Nagaoka 2007): differential-geometric framework for statistical manifolds. KL divergence as the natural divergence; Fisher information as the natural metric. Natural-gradient methods + variational inference benefit.

question.question: Compute mutual information between two binary variables
question.goal: X is a fair coin flip; Y = X with probability 0.8 (noisy copy). Compute I(X; Y).

steps.reveal: I(X; Y) = 1 - 0.722 = 0.278 bits. Y carries 0.278 bits of information about X (out of 1 possible). With p_error = 0.5 (random): I = 0. With p_error = 0 (perfect copy): I = 1.

question.question: Drag to estimate I(X; Y) when X is a fair coin + Y is X passed through a BSC with error p=0 (perfect channel).
question.explanation: Perfect channel: Y = X always, so observing Y completely determines X. I(X; Y) = H(X) = 1 bit. For BSC: I(X; Y) = 1 - H(p), where H is binary entropy. p=0 → I=1; p=0.5 → I=0; p=1 → I=1 (perfect inversion). Channel capacity is the maximum I over input distributions; for BSC with uniform input, C = I = 1 - H(p).

question.question: Classify each statement as TRUE or FALSE about KL divergence + mutual information.

items.label: D_KL satisfies triangle inequality (D_KL(P,R) ≤ D_KL(P,Q) + D_KL(Q,R))

question.explanation:
KL divergence + MI properties:
• D_KL(P || Q) ≥ 0 (Gibbs' inequality); zero iff P = Q. TRUE.
• Not symmetric: D_KL(P || Q) ≠ D_KL(Q || P) in general. FALSE.
• Zero iff equal. TRUE (Gibbs).
• I(X; Y) symmetric. TRUE.
• I(X; Y) = 0 iff X ⊥ Y. TRUE (equals D_KL(p(x,y) || p(x)p(y))).
• I(X; Y) ≤ min(H(X), H(Y)). TRUE.
• Cross-entropy H(P, Q) = H(P) + D_KL(P || Q). Cross-entropy is NOT the KL divergence; they differ by H(P). FALSE.
• KL does NOT satisfy triangle inequality. FALSE.

KL is a divergence (positive + zero iff equal) but not a metric. JS divergence + Wasserstein distance are metric alternatives. Cross-entropy + KL related but distinct.

question.question: Why is cross-entropy loss the standard for classification training (not, e.g., MSE)?
options: Cross-entropy = -∑ y_true log p_θ measures the negative log-likelihood of the true labels under the model's predicted distribution. Minimizing it = minimizing KL(P_true || P_θ) (since H(P_true) is constant in θ). MSE between probabilities + labels: lacks the proper-scoring-rule property + gives near-zero gradient when wrong with high confidence. Cross-entropy provides large gradient when confident-and-wrong → faster + more reliable convergence.
question.explanation:
**Why cross-entropy + not MSE for classification**:

*Cross-entropy loss*:
  L = -∑_i y_i log p_θ(x)_i
where y is one-hot label, p_θ are model probabilities.

*Equivalent forms*:
- Negative log-likelihood of labels.
- KL(P_true || P_θ) - H(P_true) (drop constant: minimize KL).
- Maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) of model parameters.

*Why it works for classification*:

1. **Proper scoring rule**: cross-entropy is uniquely minimized when predicted distribution matches true distribution. MSE on probabilities is a proper scoring rule but with different sensitivity.

2. **Gradient magnitude when wrong**: cross-entropy gradient ∝ (p - y) (logistic regression case) — finite + non-zero when very wrong. MSE gradient when p is wrong + saturated (e.g., p=0.999 when y=0): ~0 because sigmoid output saturates. Cross-entropy never saturates; always provides learning signal.

3. **Information-theoretic interpretation**: minimizing cross-entropy = minimizing KL = best approximation of true distribution in KL sense.

4. **Connection to softmax**: cross-entropy + softmax pair has clean gradient (p - y) — the optimization-friendly Bayes-optimal pairing.

5. **Maximum likelihood**: under iid sampling, cross-entropy minimization is asymptotically the MLE — guaranteed consistency + (under regularity) asymptotic efficiency.

*When MSE used instead*:
- Regression (continuous outputs).
- Some specific ML scenarios where calibration is critical + cross-entropy biased.
- Some Bayesian methods using posterior moments.

*Modern variants*:
- **Focal loss** (Lin+ 2017): downweights easy examples; better for imbalanced classification.
- **Label smoothing**: soft-target (1-ε on true, ε/K on others); reduces overconfidence.
- **Distillation loss**: KL between teacher + student softmax outputs.
- **Contrastive losses** (InfoNCE): MI lower-bound; foundation of CLIP + SimCLR.

*Connection back to info theory*: maximum likelihood = minimum KL = maximum information about labels in model = information bottleneck objective. The fundamental quantity is information, expressed multiple ways.

This is a key example of how information theory shapes practical ML.

hints: What's the gradient when wrong + confident?
slides.workedSolution: Cross-entropy = -∑ y log p = NLL = KL(P_true || P_θ) - H(P_true). Provides finite gradient when wrong + confident; MSE saturates near 0 + 1 → vanishing gradient. Minimizing CE = minimizing KL = MLE. Cross-entropy + softmax pair gives clean (p - y) gradient. Variants: focal loss, label smoothing, distillation, InfoNCE. Info-theoretic foundation: KL is fundamental measure of difference between distributions.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how mutual information has become a foundation for modern representation learning.
question.rubric: Mentions: I(X; Y) = bits of info Y carries about X. For representation learning: T = encoder(X); want T to retain info about Y (label) but discard nuisance variation in X. Information bottleneck (Tishby 1999): max I(T; Y) - β I(T; X). Modern self-supervised learning: CLIP, SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL use **InfoNCE** = MI lower bound between input + positive pairs. Contrastive objective: distinguish positive pair (same instance, augmented) from negative pairs; maximizes MI between representations. MINE (Belghazi+ 2018) + neural MI estimation enables direct use in objectives. CLIP: I(image, text) maximized → joint embedding. ELBOs in VAEs include KL = MI-related terms. Cross-entropy loss = KL minimization. Foundations of modern self-supervised + multimodal learning all info-theoretic. Concludes: I + KL are unifying concepts across ML.
